title: takaichis japan risks ceding policy control us 2026 09 02
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 2 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Where is Japanese monetary policy set? As far as traders are concerned, the answer is increasingly Washington. On Tuesday, yields on 10-year Japanese government bonds surpassed 3% for ​the first time in three decades, after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Japan’s central bank governor and finance ‌minister to raise interest rates on the sidelines of this week’s G20 summit, per broadcaster NHK. The longer Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi acquiesces to such pressure tactics, the less faith markets will have in her country’s capacity to chart its own financial course.
On the heels of Monday’s report, Bessent took another striking step in telling ​CNBC that “I have information that the market doesn’t have, and it’s my belief that the Japanese government and the [Bank of Japan] ​will do the things that will lead to a stronger yen.”
The bank’s ultimate decision and what Bessent really ⁠knows are both beside the point: the comments lock in market expectations that the central bank will raise rates on September 18 and ​amount to interference in a close ally’s monetary policymaking. That’s in contrast to July’s joint intervention, where Washington acted as junior partner by ​selling down its stash of euros to support the yen.
Takaichi hasn't yet spoken out against U.S. encroachment on the independence of central bank Governor Kazuo Ueda. This is probably because Bessent’s stated preference for a strong yen helps stave off greater currency weakness and keep afloat her ambitions for a 370 trillion yen ($2.3 trillion) ​investment splurge, despite investor concerns attendant bond issuance will again weaken the yen.
Of course, Japanese officials could choose to go at it alone ​and swallow the inflationary costs of currency depreciation. On Monday finance minister Satsuki Katayama played down
, opens new tab
 Bessent’s call for higher rates.
Regardless, Japan's bond market closely tracking his ‌statements reflects ⁠Tokyo surrendering some of its policy autonomy. That's a real problem because the Trump administration's aims won't always align with those of governments whose currencies it's propping up. One reason Bessent may have bought the yen, for example, is that Japan mounting a defence on its own would likely entail selling down its massive trove of U.S. bonds. But he presumably doesn't want to keep dipping into America's finite foreign-exchange pot ​either, especially since the yen has ​already walked back half its ⁠joint-intervention gains.
That might explain why, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, Bessent described “Takaichinomics” chiefly as a shareholder-friendly deregulatory drive, while suggesting Japan "should just sit back and enjoy the success of Abenomics". It's a not-so-subtle attempt ​to overwrite Takaichi's signature spendthrift agenda. Tokyo may soon discover that borrowed support comes with borrowed priorities.
